verdict.rationale: The claim that both the just and the unjust are bodily raised is grounded in a dense, pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) lexical pattern. Daniel 12:2 uses 'many' (rabbim) of those sleeping in 'soil of dust' (admat aphar), waking with the verb 'to awake' (quts), then partitioned by a doubled 'these' (eleh) into everlasting life and everlasting 'contempt' (deraon). John 5:28-29 places 'all those in the tombs' (pantes hoi en tois mnemeiois) under one 'resurrection' (anastasis) governed by twin genitives (noun forms in the 'of-X' grammatical form) 'of life' (zoes) and 'of judgment' (kriseos). Acts 24:15 makes the scope explicit by the 'both-and' (te-kai) construction coordinating 'just' (dikaion) and 'unjust' (adikon) under a single future 'resurrection' (anastasis). The witness is dense and not variant-sensitive at any cited unit, so the affirm is decisive on the both-classes claim, even though the question of one timing versus two is a separate lexical question.

scripture.force: 'Many' (rabbim) of those sleeping in 'soil of dust' (admat aphar), 'will awake' (yaqitsu). The verb 'to awake' (quts) is a physical waking from sleep, and the location is the dust of the ground, which points to bodies in the earth rather than a disembodied (without a body) state. The clause then partitions the awakened into two destinies marked by the prepositional 'to' (lamed), some to 'everlasting life' (chayye olam), and these others to 'reproaches' (chereph) and 'everlasting contempt' (deraon olam). The doubled 'these and those' (eleh) syntactically splits one waking event into a just and an unjust outcome. The word 'contempt' (deraon) is a hapax-adjacent (near-only-occurrence) hardline pair appearing only here and in Isaiah 66:24, anchoring the negative outcome to bodily corpses seen by the redeemed in Isaiah's matching scene.

An hour 'is coming' (erchetai), in which 'all those in the tombs' (pantes hoi en tois mnemeiois) will hear his voice. The universal subject 'all' (pantes) plus the locative 'in the tombs' (en tois mnemeiois) ties the rising to bodies presently in graves, which is the bodily and not merely spiritual sense. The relative clause structure under one hour sets up the partition that follows in the next verse.

Those in the tombs 'will come out' (ekporeusontai), a verb of bodily egress (coming out) from the grave. The single noun 'resurrection' (anastasis) is then qualified by two genitives (nouns in the 'of-X' grammatical form) in parallel, 'resurrection of life' (anastasin zoes) for those who did good things, and 'resurrection of judgment' (anastasin kriseos) for those who did worthless things. One resurrection word governs both groups, which encodes a single bodily rising that issues in two verdicts. The grammar here decides only that both classes rise. It does not specify whether the two 'resurrections' (anastaseis) occur in one hour or are temporally distinct (separated in time), since the singular 'hour' (hora) can be a fixed appointed time or the wider end-times (eschatological) era.

Paul professes a hope of 'a resurrection that is going to be' (anastasin esesthai), the future infinitive (the 'to be going to' verb form) with 'about to' (mellein) making this an end-times (eschatological) expectation. The single 'resurrection' (anastasis) is explicitly scoped over 'both just and unjust' (dikaion te kai adikon). The 'both-and' (te-kai) construction is a tight Greek coordinator that yokes two members under one shared noun. The grammar here is the most direct lexical statement in the canon that the unjust as well as the just are raised under one resurrection-word. It does not specify simultaneity (happening at the same time), since 'both-and' (te kai) pairs membership not timing.

'So also is the resurrection of the dead' (Houtos kai he anastasis ton nekron). The matched passive pair 'it is sown' (speiretai) and 'it is raised' (egeiretai) frames the dead body as a seed that goes into the ground and is raised, sown in 'corruption' (phthora), raised in 'incorruption' (aphtharsia). The seed and harvest framing presupposes that the same entity that is buried is the one raised, which is bodily continuity (the same body continues) rather than replacement.

'It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body' (Speiretai soma psychikon, egeiretai soma pneumatikon). The noun 'body' (soma) is retained on both sides of the contrast, so the spiritual state is still a body, not a non-bodily existence. 'Soul-animated' (psychikon) and 'Spirit-animated' (pneumatikon) are adjectives of governing mode, soul-animated versus Spirit-animated, not adjectives that remove corporeality (having a physical body). The same 'soul-animated' (psychikon) contrasts with 'Spirit-animated' (pneumatikon) in 1 Corinthians 2:14-15 where the question is mode of orientation, not material composition.

As we bore the 'image' (eikona) of the 'man of dust' (choikos), we will also bear the image of the 'heavenly one' (epouranios). The verb 'to wear or carry' (phoreo) with 'image' (eikon) ties the future state to a concrete bearing of a heavenly bodily form patterned on the risen Christ. The dust to heavenly axis echoes the 'dust' (aphar) of Daniel 12:2, joining the Hebrew and Greek witnesses on the same somatic (bodily) continuity.

Christ 'will transform' (metaschematisei) 'the body of our lowliness' (to soma tes tapeinoseos hemon), to be 'conformed' (symmorphon) to the body of his 'glory' (doxes). The retained noun 'body' (soma) plus the transformation verb confirms that the resurrection state is a glorified body, the lowly body itself reshaped rather than discarded. This corroborates (supports) the somatic (bodily) reading of 1 Corinthians 15 but speaks only of the believers' transformation, not the rising of the unjust.

The sea gave up 'the dead' (tous nekrous) in it, and death and 'Hades' (the place of the dead) gave up the dead in them, and 'they were judged' (ekrithesan), each 'according to their works' (kata ta erga auton). The dead are restored from sea and Hades before being judged, which presupposes that the unjust dead are also raised, matching the resurrection of judgment in John 5:29 and the unjust in Acts 24:15.

'Your dead shall live' (Yichyu metheka), with the imperative 'awake and sing, dwellers of dust' (haqitsu we-rannenu shokne aphar). The verb 'to live' (chayah) and 'to awake' (quts), both used of physical revival, are stacked with the locative 'dwellers of dust' (shokne aphar). The wording matches Daniel 12:2 in waking-from-dust idiom and supplies an additional Hebrew witness to bodily rising prior to its New Testament restatement.

After my 'skin' (or) has been struck off, yet from my 'flesh' (basar) I will see 'God' (eloah). The concrete bodily nouns 'skin' (or) and 'flesh' (basar) plus the verb 'to see with the eyes' (chazah) ground a future seeing of God in the body, not as a disembodied (without a body) shade. This is an early canonical foothold for bodily continuity through death into a future seeing.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase 'flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' (sarx kai haima basileian theou kleronomesai ou dunatai) could seem to deny bodily resurrection. In context 'flesh and blood' (sarx kai haima) is an idiom for mortal perishable humanity in its present corruptible mode, and the parallel clause equates it with 'corruption' (phthora) not inheriting 'incorruption' (aphtharsia). The verse denies that the perishable mode enters unchanged, not that the body is abandoned, which is consistent with the transformation language of verses 42 to 49 and Philippians 3:21.

'Spiritual body' (soma pneumatikon) could be read as immaterial (not made of matter), which would undercut bodily resurrection. The wording resists that. The head noun 'body' (soma) is retained, and 'spiritual' (pneumatikos) elsewhere in the same letter, for example 'spiritual' (pneumatikos) in 1 Corinthians 2 and 3, describes the Spirit as the animating and governing power, not the absence of matter. The matched antonym (opposite) 'soul-animated' (psychikon) names the present physical body, so 'Spirit-animated' (pneumatikon) names a Spirit-empowered body, not a ghost. Bodily resurrection stands.

'The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed' (Hoi loipoi ton nekron ouk ezesan achri telesthe ta chilia ete), immediately followed by 'this is the first resurrection' (haute he anastasis he prote). The vocabulary 'rest of the dead' (loipoi nekron) plus the temporal 'until' (achri) plus the demonstrative 'this' (haute) marking a first 'resurrection' (anastasis), lexically opens room for two distinct rising events at different times rather than one simultaneous (happening at the same time) event. This text does not undo the affirm that both classes rise, since 'rest of the dead' (loipoi nekron) presupposes their later rising. It only complicates whether the just and unjust rise at one 'hour' (hora) or at temporally separated 'resurrections' (anastaseis). The proposition under test asks only that both are raised, which all readings affirm.

'Each in his own order' (Hekastos de en to idio tagmati), with 'firstfruits Christ' (aparche Christos), 'then those of Christ at his coming' (epeita hoi tou Christou en te parousia autou), 'then the end' (eita to telos). The noun 'ordered rank' (tagma) and the temporal adverbs 'firstfruits' (aparche), 'then' (epeita), 'then' (eita), encode sequence among groups within the resurrection complex. Like Revelation 20:5, this does not deny the bodily rising of the unjust but is the lexical seedbed for ordered-stages readings of the resurrection.

variants.note: None of the cited verses fall in the ingested ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window (3 John 1:1 to 1:15). The Nestle apparatus markers visible in the surface text at John 5:28, Acts 24:15, 1 Corinthians 15:44, 15:47, 15:49, and Philippians 3:21 affect spelling, word order, and verbal aspect on 'to wear or carry' (phoreo), but they do not affect the presence of 'resurrection' (anastasis), the universal 'all' (pantes) scope, the two-destiny partition, or the retention of 'body' (soma). The verdict therefore holds across all plausible readings, and not_in_ecm_scope is the honest status.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the singular 'hour' (hora) of John 5:28-29 and the single throne scene of Revelation 20:12-13 as one resurrection of just and unjust at the end. The wording supports this since one 'resurrection' (anastasis) governs both genitives (the 'of-X' grammatical forms) 'of life' (zoes) and 'of judgment' (kriseos) in John 5:29 and the 'both-and' (te-kai) of Acts 24:15 yokes 'just' (dikaion) and 'unjust' (adikon) under one 'resurrection' (anastasis). On this reading the two destinies are sorted at one event, not at separated times.

Reads Revelation 20:5-6 as supplying a lexical distinction between 'the first resurrection' (he anastasis he prote) and the later rising of 'the rest of the dead' (hoi loipoi ton nekron), with the temporal 'until' (achri) marking the gap of the thousand years. Combined with the ordered 'ranks' (tagmata) of 1 Corinthians 15:23 and the future infinitive (the 'to be going to' verb form) 'to be' (esesthai) in Acts 24:15, this reading takes the resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment as one resurrection-word naming two temporally separated (separated in time) events. It still affirms that both just and unjust are bodily raised, which is the proposition under test.

Reads Daniel 12:2 and John 5:28-29 as one covenant-climactic event because the doubled 'these' (eleh) of Daniel 12:2 and the singular 'hour' (hora) of John 5:28 do not lexically force a temporal gap. Affirms both-classes from the 'both-and' (te-kai) of Acts 24:15.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition asks only whether both classes are bodily raised, which every defensible reading of the cited texts affirms. The disagreement is over WHEN they rise, one 'hour' (hora) versus two 'resurrections' (anastaseis) separated by the thousand years of Revelation 20, not whether the unjust rise. That timing question is decided downstream from this verdict and does not weaken the affirm here.

stem_audit.notes: The stem states a bodily resurrection of both the just and the unjust at the end of the age in plain terms and does not embed a single tradition's distinctive. The phrase end of the age is broad enough to host both one-event and two-stage readings, and the 'both-and' (te-kai) construction of Acts 24:15 is the lexical floor the stem rests on. No neutralization is required, and the verdict was derived on the original stem.

lay_summary: Across both Testaments the same vocabulary points to a future physical rising of all the dead, sorted into two outcomes. In Daniel 12:2 'many' (rabbim) of those who sleep in the 'dust' (aphar) of the earth 'awake' (quts), some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame and 'contempt' (deraon). The verb means to wake from sleep and the location is the dust of the ground, which locates this in buried bodies. Isaiah 26:19 stacks the same Hebrew words, your dead shall 'live' (chayah), awake and sing, dwellers of dust, and Job 19:26 says that from his 'flesh' (basar) he will see God. In John 5:28-29 Jesus says an 'hour' (hora) is coming when 'all those in the tombs' (pantes hoi en tois mnemeiois) hear his voice and 'come out' (ekporeuomai), one group to a 'resurrection' (anastasis) 'of life' (zoes) and the other to a resurrection 'of judgment' (kriseos). One word for resurrection covers both groups, so a single rising leads to two verdicts. Paul restates the same hope in Acts 24:15, a resurrection of 'both just and unjust' (dikaion te kai adikon), where a tight Greek 'both-and' (te-kai) pairing yokes both classes under one rising. In 1 Corinthians 15 the dead body is described like a seed that is 'sown' (speiro) and then 'raised' (egeiro), sown in 'corruption' (phthora) and raised in 'incorruption' (aphtharsia), sown a 'natural body' (soma psychikon) and raised a 'spiritual body' (soma pneumatikon). The word 'body' (soma) is kept on both sides, so the raised state is still a body but one transformed and ruled by the Spirit, not a ghost. Philippians 3:21 adds that the lowly body itself is reshaped to match the glory of the risen Christ. Where readers differ is whether the just and the unjust rise at the same hour or at two separated events. Revelation 20:5 says 'the rest of the dead' (loipoi nekron) did not live until the thousand years were completed, calling the earlier rising the 'first resurrection' (anastasis prote), and 1 Corinthians 15:23 names ordered 'ranks' (tagmata). Those texts open the timing question, but they do not unsettle the claim that both classes are bodily raised, which the words in every cited passage support.

license_audit.non_redistributable_reason: Two sources carry the non-commercial CC-BY-NC-4.0 license and cannot be bulk redistributed: MACULA-Greek (used for syntactic framing of 1 Corinthians 15:42 and the 'both-and' (te-kai) construction in Acts 24:15) and ETCBC-BHSA (used for the clause and function analysis of Daniel 12:2). The remaining sources are individually redistributable, but the aggregate is gated by these two.
